claim: A total of 539,134 altORFs were predicted compared to 68,264 annotated CDSs in the human transcriptome.
source: We predicted a total of 539,134 altORFs compared to 68,264 annotated CDSs in the human transcriptome (Figure 1b, Table 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data presented in Figure 1b and Table 1.

claim: The number of unique altORFs and CDSs becomes 183,191 and 54,498, respectively, when accounting for identical ORFs in different RNA isoforms.
source: Because identical ORFs can be present in different RNA isoforms transcribed from the same genomic locus, the number of unique altORFs and CDSs becomes 183,191 and 54,498, respectively.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and represents data analysis results.

claim: The median size of predicted human alternative proteins is 45 amino acids compared to 460 for reference proteins.
source: The median alternative protein length is 45 amino acids (AA) compared to 460 for the reference proteins.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1c.

claim: 92.96% of alternative proteins have less than 100 amino acids.
source: Thus, the bulk of the translation products of altORFs would be small proteins.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text following the size distribution analysis.

claim: The majority of altORFs either overlap annotated CDSs in a different reading frame (35.98%) or are located in 3'UTRs (40.09%).
source: The majority of altORFs either overlap annotated CDSs in a different reading frame (35.98%) or are located in 3'UTRs (40.09%) (Figure 1d).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1d.

claim: 9.83% of altORFs are located in repeat sequences.
source: 9.83% of altORFs are located in repeat sequences (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a), compared to 2.45% of CDSs.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: 62,307 more altORFs were observed than would be expected from random occurrence alone.
source: Overall, we observed 62,307 more altORFs than would be expected from random occurrence alone (Figure 1e; p<0.0001).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1e.

claim: The density of altORFs observed in the CDSs, 3'UTRs and ncRNAs was markedly higher than in the shuffled transcriptomes.
source: The density of altORFs observed in the CDSs, 3'UTRs and ncRNAs (Figure 1f) was markedly higher than in the shuffled transcriptomes, suggesting that these are maintained at frequencies higher than expected by chance, again potentially due to their coding function.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1f.

claim: The density of altORFs observed in 5'UTRs was much lower than in the shuffled transcriptomes.
source: In contrast, the density of altORFs observed in 5'UTRs was much lower than in the shuffled transcriptomes, supporting recent claims that negative selection eliminates AUGs (and thus the potential for the evolution of altORFs) in these regions (Iacono et al., 2005; Neafsey and Galagan, 2007).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by comparison to shuffled transcriptomes and citations.

claim: 27,539 (15% of 183,191) human altORFs encoding predicted alternative proteins have a Kozak motif (A/GNNAUGG).
source: We find that 27,539 (15% of 183,191) human altORFs encoding predicted alternative proteins have a Kozak motif (A/GNNAUGG), as compared to 19,745 (36% of 54,498) for annotated CDSs encoding reference proteins (Figure 1g).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1g.

claim: 19,745 (36% of 54,498) annotated CDSs encoding reference proteins have a Kozak motif.
source: We find that 27,539 (15% of 183,191) human altORFs encoding predicted alternative proteins have a Kozak motif (A/GNNAUGG), as compared to 19,745 (36% of 54,498) for annotated CDSs encoding reference proteins (Figure 1g).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1g.

claim: The number of altORFs with Kozak motifs is significantly higher in the human transcriptome compared to shuffled transcriptomes.
source: The number of altORFs with Kozak motifs is significantly higher in the human transcriptome compared to shuffled transcriptomes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), again supporting their potential role as protein coding.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by statistical comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: In mammals, the number of homologous alternative proteins is higher than the number of homologous reference proteins.
source: In mammals, the number of homologous alternative proteins is higher than the number of homologous reference proteins (Figure 2a), and nine are even conserved from human to yeast (Figure 2b), supporting a potential functional role.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2a.

claim: Nine alternative proteins are conserved from human to yeast.
source: In mammals, the number of homologous alternative proteins is higher than the number of homologous reference proteins (Figure 2a), and nine are even conserved from human to yeast (Figure 2b), supporting a potential functional role.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2b.

claim: As phylogenetic distance from human increases, the number and percentage of genes encoding homologous alternative proteins decreases more rapidly than the percentage of genes encoding reference proteins.
source: As phylogenetic distance from human increases, the number and percentage of genes encoding homologous alternative proteins decreases more rapidly than the percentage of genes encoding reference proteins (Figure 2a and c).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Figures 2a and 2c.

claim: In regions of the CDS overlapping altORFs, third codon positions were evolving at significantly more extreme speeds (slow or quick) than third codon positions of random control sequences from the entire CDS.
source: We observed that in regions of the CDS overlapping altORFs, third codon positions were evolving at significantly more extreme speeds (slow or quick) than third codon positions of random control sequences from the entire CDS (Figure 3), reaching up to 67-fold for conservation at p<0.0001 and 124-fold for accelerated evolution at p<0.0001.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: 26,531 TISs mapping to annotated CDSs and 12,616 mapping to altORFs were detected in ribosome profiling studies.
source: We re-analyzed detected TISs in publicly available ribosome profiling data (Michel et al., 2014; Raj et al., 2016), and found 26,531 TISs mapping to annotated CDSs and 12,616 mapping to altORFs in these studies (Figure 5a; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by re-analysis of published data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: 3957 predicted alternative proteins were detected in the interactome of reference proteins.
source: In the first dataset, we detected 3957 predicted alternative proteins in the interactome of reference proteins (Hein et al., 2015), providing a framework to uncover the function of these proteins.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and based on re-analysis of published proteomic data.

claim: 549 predicted alternative proteins were detected in a proteomic dataset containing about 10,000 reference human proteins.
source: In a second proteomic dataset containing about 10,000 reference human proteins (Rosenberger et al., 2014), a total of 549 predicted alternative proteins were detected.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and based on re-analysis of published proteomic data.

claim: 384 alternative proteins were detected using a phosphoproteomic large data set.
source: Using a phosphoproteomic large data set (Sharma et al., 2014), we detected 384 alternative proteins.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and based on re-analysis of published proteomic data.

claim: 77 alternative proteins were detected in the epidermal growth factor receptor interactome.
source: A fourth proteomic dataset contained 77 alternative proteins in the epidermal growth factor receptor interactome (Tong et al., 2014) (Figure 5b).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and based on re-analysis of published proteomic data.

claim: A total of 4872 different alternative proteins were detected in proteomic data.
source: A total of 4872 different alternative proteins were detected in these proteomic data.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and represents the combined results from multiple proteomic datasets.

claim: 467 alternative proteins were detected by both MS and ribosome profiling.
source: 467 of these alternative proteins were detected by both MS and ribosome profiling (Figure 7), providing a high-confidence collection of small alternative proteins for further studies.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7.

claim: 41,511 (23%) human alternative proteins have at least one InterPro signature.
source: We found 41,511 (23%) human alternative proteins with at least one InterPro signature (Figure 8b).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 8b.

claim: 37,739 (or 20.6%) alternative proteins with InterPro signatures are classified as small proteins.
source: Of these, 37,739 (or 20.6%) are classified as small proteins.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text following the InterPro analysis.

claim: The reference proteome has a smaller proportion (840 or 1.68%) of small proteins with at least one InterPro signature.
source: Interestingly, the reference proteome has a smaller proportion (840 or 1.68%) of small proteins with at least one InterPro signature, supporting a biological activity for alternative proteins.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and used to support the biological activity of alternative proteins.

claim: More than 15,000 alternative proteins have signatures linked to membrane proteins.
source: Similar to reference proteins, signatures linked to membrane proteins are abundant in the alternative proteome and represent more than 15,000 proteins (Figure 8c–e; Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Figures 8c-e and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Most of the alternative proteins with a signal peptide do not have a transmembrane segment and are predicted to be secreted.
source: Most of the alternative proteins with a signal peptide do not have a transmembrane segment and are predicted to be secreted (Figure 8c,d), supporting the presence of large numbers of alternative proteins in plasma (Vanderperre et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Figures 8c and 8d, with additional citation support.

claim: The majority of predicted alternative proteins with transmembrane domains have a single membrane spanning domain but some display up to 27 transmembrane regions.
source: The majority of predicted alternative proteins with transmembrane domains have a single membrane spanning domain but some display up to 27 transmembrane regions, which is still within the range of reference proteins that show a maximum of 33 (Figure 8e).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 8e.

claim: A total of 585 alternative proteins were assigned 419 different InterPro entries.
source: A total of 585 alternative proteins were assigned 419 different InterPro entries, and 343 of them were tentatively assigned 192 gene ontology terms (Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 9.

claim: 343 alternative proteins were tentatively assigned 192 gene ontology terms.
source: A total of 585 alternative proteins were assigned 419 different InterPro entries, and 343 of them were tentatively assigned 192 gene ontology terms (Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 9.

claim: 15.5% (91/585) of alternative proteins with an InterPro entry were detected by MS or/and ribosome profiling, compared to 13.7% (22,055/161,110) for alternative proteins without an InterPro entry.
source: 15.5% (91/585) of alternative proteins with an InterPro entry were detected by MS or/and ribosome profiling, compared to 13.7% (22,055/161,110) for alternative proteins without an InterPro entry (p-value=1.13e-05, Fisher's exact test and chi-square test).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by statistical analysis.

claim: 110 alternative proteins contain C2H2 zinc finger domains.
source: The most abundant class of predicted alternative proteins with at least one InterPro entry are C2H2 zinc finger proteins with 110 alternative proteins containing 187 C2H2-type/integrase DNA-binding domains, 91 C2H2 domains and 23 C2H2-like domains (Figure 10a).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 10a.

claim: Eighteen of the 110 alternative zinc finger proteins (17.8%) were detected in public proteomic and ribosome profiling datasets.
source: Eighteen of these (17.8%) were detected in public proteomic and ribosome profiling datasets (Table 2), a percentage that is similar to reference zinc finger proteins (20.1%).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Table 2.

claim: Alternative proteins have between 1 and 23 zinc finger domains.
source: Alternative proteins have between 1 and 23 zinc finger domains (Figure 10b).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 10b.

claim: The consensus TGEK linker is present 46 times in 31 alternative zinc finger proteins.
source: The consensus TGEK linker is present 46 times in 31 alternative zinc finger proteins (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Supplementary file 4.

claim: 138 pairs of alternative and reference proteins have at least one identical InterPro entry.
source: Overall, 138 alternative/reference protein pairs have at least one identical InterPro entry and many pairs have more than one identical entry (Figure 11a).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 11a.

claim: The number of identical entries was much higher than expected by chance.
source: The number of identical entries was much higher than expected by chance (Figure 11b, p<0.0001).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 11b.

claim: 89 of 110 altORFs coding for zinc finger proteins are present in transcripts in which the CDS also codes for a zinc finger protein.
source: Strikingly, 89 of 110 altORFs coding for zinc finger proteins (Figure 10) are present in transcripts in which the CDS also codes for a zinc finger protein.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and refers to Figure 10.

claim: Five alternative proteins (IP_168460.1, IP_168527.1, IP_270697.1, IP_273983.1, IP_279784.1) were identified within the interactome of their reference zinc finger proteins.
source: Five alternative proteins (IP_168460.1, IP_168527.1, IP_270697.1, IP_273983.1, IP_279784.1) were identified within the interactome of their reference zinc finger proteins.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and based on re-analysis of MS data.

claim: The number of interactions between alternative zinc finger proteins and their reference proteins was higher than expected by chance (p<10−6).
source: This number was higher than expected by chance (p<10−6) based on 1 million binomial simulations of randomized interactomes.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by statistical simulation.

claim: 2715 alternative proteins are predicted to have a function in mammals (H. sapiens to B. taurus).
source: Finally, we integrated the expression analyses and the conservation analyses of alternative/reference protein pairs to produce a high-confidence list of alternative proteins predicted to have a function and found 2715 alternative proteins in mammals (H. sapiens to B. taurus), and 44 in vertebrates (H. sapiens to D. rerio) (Supplementary file 7).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Supplementary file 7.

claim: 44 alternative proteins are predicted to have a function in vertebrates (H. sapiens to D. rerio).
source: Finally, we integrated the expression analyses and the conservation analyses of alternative/reference protein pairs to produce a high-confidence list of alternative proteins predicted to have a function and found 2715 alternative proteins in mammals (H. sapiens to B. taurus), and 44 in vertebrates (H. sapiens to D. rerio) (Supplementary file 7).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Supplementary file 7.

claim: AltMiD51 is a 70 amino acid alternative protein conserved in vertebrates.
source: AltMiD51 is a 70 amino acid alternative protein conserved in vertebrates (Andreev et al., 2015) and conserved with its reference protein MiD51 from humans to zebrafish (Supplementary file 7).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by citation and Supplementary file 7.

claim: AltMiD51 is robustly detected by MS in several cell lines.
source: Yet, altMiD51 is robustly detected by MS in several cell lines (Supplementary file 2: HEK293, HeLa Kyoto, HeLa S3, THP1 cells and gut tissue), and we validated some spectra using synthetic peptides (Figure 12—figure supplement 1), and it is also detected by ribosome profiling (Supplementary file 1) (Vanderperre et al., 2013; Andreev et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by MS data, synthetic peptide validation, and citations.

claim: AltMiD51 localizes at the mitochondria.
source: Remarkably, we found that altMiD51 also localizes at the mitochondria (Figure 12c; Figure 12—figure supplement 3) and that its overexpression results in mitochondrial fission (Figure 12d).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Figures 12c and Figure 12—figure supplement 3.

claim: Overexpression of altMiD51 results in mitochondrial fission.
source: Remarkably, we found that altMiD51 also localizes at the mitochondria (Figure 12c; Figure 12—figure supplement 3) and that its overexpression results in mitochondrial fission (Figure 12d).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 12d.

claim: The LYR domain is essential for altMiD51-induced mitochondrial fission.
source: The LYR domain is essential for altMiD51-induced mitochondrial fission since a mutant of the LYR domain, altMiD51(LYR→AAA) was unable to convert the mitochondrial morphology from tubular to fragmented (Figure 12d).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 12d.

claim: Drp1(K38A), a dominant negative mutant of Drp1, largely prevented the ability of altMiD51 to induce mitochondrial fragmentation.
source: Drp1(K38A), a dominant negative mutant of Drp1 (Smirnova et al., 1998), largely prevented the ability of altMiD51 to induce mitochondrial fragmentation (Figure 12d; Figure 12—figure supplement 5a).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 12d and Figure 12—figure supplement 5a, with citation support.

claim: Drp1 knockdown interfered with altMiD51-induced mitochondrial fragmentation.
source: Drp1 knockdown interfered with altMiD51-induced mitochondrial fragmentation (Figure 13), confirming the proposition that Drp1 mediates altMiD51-induced mitochondrial fragmentation.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 13.

claim: AltDDIT3 is a 31 amino acid alternative protein conserved in vertebrates.
source: AltDDIT3 is a 31 amino acid alternative protein conserved in vertebrates and conserved with its reference protein DDIT3 from human to bovine (Supplementary file 7).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Supplementary file 7.

claim: Both altDDIT3 and DDIT3 were mainly localized in the nucleus and partially localized in the cytoplasm.
source: Interestingly, both proteins were mainly localized in the nucleus and partially localized in the cytoplasm (Figure 14b).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 14b.

claim: AltDDIT3 and DDIT3 co-localize in the nucleus and cytoplasm (Pearson correlation coefficient 0.92).
source: Both proteins seemed to co-localize in these two compartments (Pearson correlation coefficient 0.92, Figure 14c).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 14c.

claim: DDIT3mCherry was immunoprecipitated with GFP-trap agarose in lysates from cells co-expressing altDDIT3GFP and DDIT3mCherry, confirming an interaction between the two proteins.
source: Finally, in lysates from cells co-expressing altDDIT3GFP and DDIT3mCherry, DDIT3mCherry was immunoprecipitated with GFP-trap agarose, confirming an interaction between the small altDDTI3 and the large DDIT3 proteins encoded in the same gene (Figure 14e).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 14e.

claim: Current protein databases are based on the assumption that a mature mRNA contains a single CDS.
source: In particular, a mature mRNA is predicted to contain a single CDS; yet, ribosomes can select more than one translation initiation site (TIS) (Ingolia et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2012; Mouilleron et al., 2016) on any single mRNA.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by citations.

claim: Ribosomes can select more than one translation initiation site (TIS) on any single mRNA.
source: In particular, a mature mRNA is predicted to contain a single CDS; yet, ribosomes can select more than one translation initiation site (TIS) (Ingolia et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2012; Mouilleron et al., 2016) on any single mRNA.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by citations.

claim: Minimum size limits imposed on the length of CDSs result in many RNAs being mistakenly classified as non-coding (ncRNAs).
source: Also, minimum size limits are imposed on the length of CDSs, resulting in many RNAs being mistakenly classified as non-coding (ncRNAs) (Pauli et al., 2014; Anderson et al., 2015; Zanet et al., 2015; Nelson et al., 2016; Bazzini et al., 2014; Ji et al., 2015; Prabakaran et al., 2014; Slavoff et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by multiple citations.

claim: The size and complexity of most eukaryotic proteomes have probably been greatly underestimated.
source: As a result of these assumptions, the size and complexity of most eukaryotic proteomes have probably been greatly underestimated (Andrews and Rothnagel, 2014; Landry et al., 2015; Fields et al., 2015; Saghatelian and Couso, 2015).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by citations.

claim: Few small proteins (defined as of 100 amino acids or less) are annotated in current databases.
source: In particular, few small proteins (defined as of 100 amino acids or less) are annotated in current databases.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and represents a known limitation of current databases.

claim: The absence of annotation of small proteins is a major bottleneck in the study of their function and their roles in health and disease.
source: The absence of annotation of small proteins is a major bottleneck in the study of their function and their roles in health and disease.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and represents an inference about the impact of missing annotations.

claim: Many critical regulatory molecules are small proteins, such as the F0 subunit of the F0F1-ATPsynthase, phospholamban, and hepcidin.
source: This is further supported by classical and recent examples of small proteins of functional importance, for instance many critical regulatory molecules such as the F0 subunit of the F0F1-ATPsynthase (Stock et al., 1999), the sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase regulator phospholamban (Schmitt et al., 2003), and the key regulator of iron homeostasis hepcidin (Nemeth et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by citations.

claim: New genes generally code for small proteins.
source: Because these genes generally code for small proteins (Carvunis et al., 2012; Schlötterer, 2015; McLysaght and Hurst, 2016; Sabath et al., 2012), they are difficult to unambiguously detect by proteomics and in fact are impossible to detect if they are not included in proteomics databases.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by citations.

claim: An unknown fraction of small ORFs may occur by chance in the transcriptome, generating a significant level of noise.
source: Functional annotation of ORFs encoding small proteins is particularly challenging since an unknown fraction of small ORFs may occur by chance in the transcriptome, generating a significant level of noise (Landry et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by citation.

claim: Many small proteins have important functions and are ultimately one of the most important sources of functional novelty.
source: However, given that many small proteins have important functions and are ultimately one of the most important sources of functional novelty, it is time to address the challenge of their functional annotations (Landry et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by citation.

claim: AltORFs are defined as potential protein-coding ORFs in ncRNAs, in UTRs or in different reading frames from annotated CDSs in mRNAs.
source: Here, altORFs are defined as potential protein-coding ORFs in ncRNAs, in UTRs or in different reading frames from annotated CDSs in mRNAs (Figure 1a).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: The overexpression of altMiD51 did not change oxygen consumption nor ATP and reactive oxygen species production.
source: This activity is unlikely to be through perturbation of oxidative phosphorylation since the overexpression of altMiD51 did not change oxygen consumption nor ATP and reactive oxygen species production (Figure 12—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 12—figure supplement 4.

claim: The decrease in spare respiratory capacity in altMiD51-expressing cells likely resulted from mitochondrial fission.
source: The decrease in spare respiratory capacity in altMiD51-expressing cells (Figure 12—figure supplement 4a) likely resulted from mitochondrial fission (Motori et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by experimental data and citation.

claim: The tripeptide LYR motif predicted with InterProScan and located in the N-terminal domain of altMiD51 is a signature of mitochondrial proteins localized in the mitochondrial matrix.
source: Importantly, the tripeptide LYR motif predicted with InterProScan and located in the N-terminal domain of altMiD51 (Figure 12a) is a signature of mitochondrial proteins localized in the mitochondrial matrix (Angerer, 2015).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by InterProScan prediction and citation.

claim: MiD51/MIEF1/SMCR7L encodes the mitochondrial protein MiD51, which promotes mitochondrial fission by recruiting cytosolic Drp1 to mitochondria.
source: Since MiD51/MIEF1/SMCR7L encodes the mitochondrial protein MiD51, which promotes mitochondrial fission by recruiting cytosolic Drp1, a member of the dynamin family of large GTPases, to mitochondria (Losón et al., 2013), we tested for a possible functional connection between these two proteins expressed from the same mRNA.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by citation.

claim: MiD51 induces mitochondrial fission.
source: We first confirmed that MiD51 induces mitochondrial fission (Figure 12—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 12—figure supplement 2.

claim: Co-expression of wild-type Drp1 and altMiD51 proteins resulted in mitochondrial fragmentation.
source: In a control experiment, co-expression of wild-type Drp1 and altMiD51 proteins resulted in mitochondrial fragmentation (Figure 12—figure supplement 5b).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 12—figure supplement 5b.

claim: Drp1 is the key player mediating mitochondrial fission and most likely mediates altMiD51-induced mitochondrial fragmentation.
source: However, Drp1 is the key player mediating mitochondrial fission and most likely mediates altMiD51-induced mitochondrial fragmentation, as indicated by our results.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and based on inference from experimental results.

claim: The altORF encoding altDDIT3 was characterized as an inhibitory upstream ORF.
source: Interestingly, the altORF5' encoding altDDIT3 was characterized as an inhibitory upstream ORF (Jousse et al., 2001; Young et al., 2016), but evidence of endogenous expression of the corresponding small protein was not sought.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by citations.

claim: The detection of altMiD51 and altDDIT3 suggests that a fraction of altORFs5' may have dual functions as translation regulators and functional proteins.
source: The detection of altMiD51 and altDDIT3 suggests that a fraction of altORFs5' may have dual functions as translation regulators and functional proteins.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and represents an inference from the detection of these proteins.

claim: A first possible mechanism for the evolutionary origins of altORFs involves the polymorphism of initiation and stop codons during evolution.
source: A first possible mechanism involves the polymorphism of initiation and stop codons during evolution (Lee and Reinhardt, 2012; Andreatta et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by citations.

claim: The generation of an early stop codon in the 5'end of a CDS could be followed by the evolution of another translation initiation site downstream, creating a new independent ORF in the 3'UTR of the canonical gene.
source: For instance, the generation of an early stop codon in the 5'end of a CDS could be followed by the evolution of another translation initiation site downstream, creating a new independent ORF in the 3'UTR of the canonical gene.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and represents a speculative mechanism.

claim: This mechanism of altORF origin would produce a new altORF that has identical protein domains with the annotated CDS, as observed for 24% of the 585 alternative proteins with an InterPro entry.
source: This mechanism of altORF origin, reminiscent of gene fission, would at the same time produce a new altORF that has identical protein domains with the annotated CDS, as we observed for a substantial fraction (24%) of the 585 alternative proteins with an InterPro entry.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by data analysis.

claim: A second mechanism for altORF origin would be de novo origin of ORFs, following established models of gene evolution de novo.
source: A second mechanism would be de novo origin of ORFs, which would follow the well-established models of gene evolution de novo (Schlötterer, 2015; Knowles and McLysaght, 2009; Neme and Tautz, 2013) in which new ORFs are transcribed and translated and have new functions or await the evolution of new functions by mutations.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by citations.

claim: The numerous altORFs with no detectable protein domains may have originated from previously non-coding regions or in regions that completely overlap with CDS in other reading frames.
source: The numerous altORFs with no detectable protein domains may have originated this way from previously non-coding regions or in regions that completely overlap with CDS in other reading frames.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and represents a speculative inference.

claim: A TIS detected by ribosome profiling does not necessarily imply that the protein is expressed as a stable molecule.
source: A TIS detected by ribosome profiling does not necessarily imply that the protein is expressed as a stable molecule, and proteomic analyses more readily detect large proteins that generate several peptides after enzymatic digestion.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and represents a known limitation of ribosome profiling.

claim: Proteomic analyses more readily detect large proteins that generate several peptides after enzymatic digestion.
source: A TIS detected by ribosome profiling does not necessarily imply that the protein is expressed as a stable molecule, and proteomic analyses more readily detect large proteins that generate several peptides after enzymatic digestion.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and represents a known limitation of proteomics.

claim: Evolutionarily novel genes tend to be poorly expressed, reducing the probability of detection.
source: In addition, evolutionarily novel genes tend to be poorly expressed, again reducing the probability of detection (Schlötterer, 2015).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by citation.

claim: The use of a combination of five search engines increases the confidence and sensitivity of hits compared to single-search-engine processing.
source: Here, we used a combination of five search engines, thus increasing the confidence and sensitivity of hits compared to single-search-engine processing (Vaudel et al., 2015; Shteynberg et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by citations.

claim: Only a relatively small percentage of alternative proteins (22.6%) are functionally annotated with Interpro signatures, compared to reference proteins (96.9%).
source: Only a relatively small percentage of alternative proteins (22.6%) are functionally annotated with Interpro signatures, compared to reference proteins (96.9%).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and represents data analysis results.

claim: The small size of alternative proteins with a median size of 45 amino acids may not be able to accommodate large domains.
source: An obvious explanation is the small size of alternative proteins with a median size of 45 amino acids, which may not be able to accommodate large domains.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and represents an inference about the relationship between protein size and domain presence.

claim: Small proteins may be precursors of new proteins but require an elongation of their coding sequence before they display a useful cellular activity.
source: It has been proposed that small proteins may be precursors of new proteins but require an elongation of their coding sequence before they display a useful cellular activity (Carvunis et al., 2012; Couso and Patraquim, 2017).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by citations.

claim: Protein domains may appear only after elongation of the coding sequence.
source: According to this hypothesis, it is possible that protein domains appear only after elongation of the coding sequence.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and represents a speculative inference.

claim: InterPro domains were identified by investigating the reference proteome, and alternative proteins may have new domains and motifs that remain to be characterized.
